questions.title: AI strategy for software engineering
questions.text: Is there a documented AI strategy for software engineering that is sponsored by leadership, states explicit goals, and is communicated to every engineering team?
questions.l3: Strategy published and reviewed at least yearly; goals (for example delivery, quality, developer experience) have owners; most engineers can say where to find it.
questions.l4: Strategy is revised from measured results (D9) and linked to business OKRs; progress is reported to leadership on a fixed cadence.
questions.evidence_examples: Strategy document, leadership communication, OKR entries.

questions.title: Acceptable-use policy
questions.text: Is it clear to engineers how they are and are not allowed to use AI at work, including which data can be shared with AI tools?
questions.l3: Written acceptable-use policy covers code, customer data, secrets and third-party IP; it is part of onboarding; exceptions have an owner.
questions.l4: Policy is enforced by technical controls (for example content exclusion, data loss prevention, allowlists) and audited; violations trigger automated alerts.
questions.evidence_examples: Policy link, onboarding checklist, control configuration.

questions.title: Approved tools and models
questions.text: Is there a maintained catalog of approved AI tools, features and models for software development, managed through enterprise or organization policies?
questions.l3: Enterprise/organization policies enable only approved features and models; the catalog lists owner, data handling and review date for each tool.
questions.l4: New models and tools go through a defined evaluation per task type (quality, cost, security) before enablement; retired ones are removed on schedule.
questions.evidence_examples: Copilot policy settings, tool catalog, model evaluation records.

questions.title: Data protection, IP and residency
questions.text: Are data residency, retention, intellectual property and privacy requirements defined and applied to the AI tools and agents used in the SDLC?
questions.l3: Requirements are documented per tool; sensitive repositories or files are excluded from AI context; logs and memory retention follow policy.
questions.l4: Compliance is assessed continuously (for example with a compliance manager) and mapped to regulations such as the EU AI Act where applicable.
questions.evidence_examples: Data processing records, exclusion settings, retention policy.

questions.title: Autonomy levels for AI work
questions.text: Has the organization defined which tasks are developer-led, developer-with-agent, or fully agent-led, and the controls required for each level?
questions.l3: A published matrix maps task types (for example dependency upgrades, test generation, feature work, production changes) to autonomy levels and required approvals.
questions.l4: The matrix is enforced by platform rules (for example branch protection, required reviewers per path) and updated from incident and quality data.
questions.evidence_examples: Autonomy matrix, repository rulesets, change records.

questions.title: Responsible AI and risk framework
questions.text: Is AI use in software engineering governed by a responsible AI standard and a recognized risk framework (for example Microsoft Responsible AI Standard, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001)?
questions.l3: A named framework is adopted; AI-related risks are in the risk register with owners and reviews.
questions.l4: Framework controls are audited internally or externally; results feed back into policy and tooling.
questions.evidence_examples: Framework mapping, risk register entries, audit reports.

questions.title: Agent registry and identity
questions.text: Is every AI agent used in the SDLC (coding agents, review agents, custom agents, pipeline agents) registered with an owner, a purpose, a distinct identity and a defined access scope?
questions.l3: A single inventory lists all agents with owner, platform and permissions; each agent runs under its own identity, not a shared human account.
questions.l4: Unregistered ("shadow") agents are detected automatically; identity lifecycle (creation, review, removal) is automated.
questions.evidence_examples: Agent inventory, identity configuration (for example Microsoft Entra Agent ID), access reviews.

questions.title: Structured AI training
questions.text: Do engineers receive structured training on the approved AI tools and agent workflows, beyond the vendor's default onboarding?
questions.l3: Role-based curriculum (developer, reviewer, platform, security) with completion tracked; training is required before agent features are enabled; it teaches learning-preserving patterns (ask for explanations, attempt first, then compare) and not only full delegation.
questions.l4: Curriculum is updated each quarter from usage data and failure patterns; advanced tracks exist (agent orchestration, evaluation).
questions.evidence_examples: Learning paths, completion rates, enablement gating rules.

questions.title: Peer learning and champions
questions.text: Are there regular peer-learning formats (demos, brown bags, office hours) and a network of AI champions across teams?
questions.l3: Champions exist in most teams; sessions run at least monthly; recordings and examples are shared in one place.
questions.l4: A community of practice curates reusable assets (instructions, prompt files, agents) and measures their reuse.
questions.evidence_examples: Champion list, session calendar, shared repository of examples.

questions.title: Support for experimentation
questions.text: Does the organization give engineers time, sandboxes and budget to experiment safely with new AI tools and agent patterns?
questions.l3: Sandboxed environments and a lightweight request path exist; experiments are logged and their results shared.
questions.l4: Successful experiments move into the approved catalog (D1-Q3) through a defined path within weeks.
questions.evidence_examples: Sandbox subscriptions, experiment log, promotion records.

questions.title: Context-engineering skills

questions.l4: Context practices are measured (for example success rate or token use per task) and improved over time.
questions.evidence_examples: Guidance pages, review checklists, before/after metrics.

questions.title: Roles and career paths

questions.l3: Updated role profiles are published; performance reviews recognize effective AI use and review quality, not raw output volume.
questions.l4: Dedicated roles exist (for example AI engineer, agent platform owner) with a clear growth path.
questions.evidence_examples: Career framework, role descriptions.

questions.title: Depth of AI use across surfaces
questions.text: How deeply do engineers use AI across surfaces: completions and agent edits in the IDE, GitHub agent surfaces (cloud agent, code review, CLI), and several agents together?
questions.l3: Many engineers regularly use at least one GitHub agent surface ("Agent first"), confirmed by usage metrics.
questions.l4: Multi-agent use is normal ("Multi-agent"), with cohort distribution tracked monthly.
questions.evidence_examples: Copilot usage metrics dashboard or API: adoption cohort distribution, daily/weekly active users.

questions.title: Agent mode for multi-file work
questions.text: Do engineers use IDE agent mode (or equivalent) for multi-file changes, and review every change before committing?
questions.l3: Agent mode is the default for multi-file refactors and features in most teams; changes are reviewed in the diff before commit.
questions.l4: Teams share agent-mode patterns that work and track where it fails; tool permissions are tuned per repository.

questions.title: Coding agent delegation
questions.text: Are coding agents (for example Copilot cloud agent) assigned issues and producing pull requests that are merged after human review?

questions.l4: Agent PR merge rate, rework and post-merge fix rate are tracked by task type; delegation rules (D1-Q5) are tuned from this data.
questions.evidence_examples: Agent-authored PR counts, merge rate, time to merge, follow-up fixes.

questions.title: Repository instructions

questions.l4: Instructions are generated from a shared baseline, checked for staleness, and their effect on agent merge rate and code quality is measured, since instruction files alone do not guarantee better results.

questions.title: AI strategy for software engineering
questions.text: Is there a documented AI strategy for software engineering that is sponsored by leadership, states explicit goals, and is communicated to every engineering team?
questions.l3: Strategy published and reviewed at least yearly; goals (for example delivery, quality, developer experience) have owners; most engineers can say where to find it.
questions.l4: Strategy is revised from measured results (D9) and linked to business OKRs; progress is reported to leadership on a fixed cadence.
questions.evidence_examples: Strategy document, leadership communication, OKR entries.

questions.title: Acceptable-use policy
questions.text: Is it clear to engineers how they are and are not allowed to use AI at work, including which data can be shared with AI tools?
questions.l3: Written acceptable-use policy covers code, customer data, secrets and third-party IP; it is part of onboarding; exceptions have an owner.
questions.l4: Policy is enforced by technical controls (for example content exclusion, data loss prevention, allowlists) and audited; violations trigger automated alerts.
questions.evidence_examples: Policy link, onboarding checklist, control configuration.

questions.title: Approved tools and models
questions.text: Is there a maintained catalog of approved AI tools, features and models for software development, managed through enterprise or organization policies?
questions.l3: Enterprise/organization policies enable only approved features and models; the catalog lists owner, data handling and review date for each tool.
questions.l4: New models and tools go through a defined evaluation per task type (quality, cost, security) before enablement; retired ones are removed on schedule.
questions.evidence_examples: Copilot policy settings, tool catalog, model evaluation records.

questions.title: Data protection, IP and residency
questions.text: Are data residency, retention, intellectual property and privacy requirements defined and applied to the AI tools and agents used in the SDLC?
questions.l3: Requirements are documented per tool; sensitive repositories or files are excluded from AI context; logs and memory retention follow policy.
questions.l4: Compliance is assessed continuously (for example with a compliance manager) and mapped to regulations such as the EU AI Act where applicable.
questions.evidence_examples: Data processing records, exclusion settings, retention policy.

questions.title: Autonomy levels for AI work
questions.text: Has the organization defined which tasks are developer-led, developer-with-agent, or fully agent-led, and the controls required for each level?
questions.l3: A published matrix maps task types (for example dependency upgrades, test generation, feature work, production changes) to autonomy levels and required approvals.
questions.l4: The matrix is enforced by platform rules (for example branch protection, required reviewers per path) and updated from incident and quality data.
questions.evidence_examples: Autonomy matrix, repository rulesets, change records.

questions.title: Responsible AI and risk framework
questions.text: Is AI use in software engineering governed by a responsible AI standard and a recognized risk framework (for example Microsoft Responsible AI Standard, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001)?
questions.l3: A named framework is adopted; AI-related risks are in the risk register with owners and reviews.
questions.l4: Framework controls are audited internally or externally; results feed back into policy and tooling.
questions.evidence_examples: Framework mapping, risk register entries, audit reports.

questions.title: Agent registry and identity
questions.text: Is every AI agent used in the SDLC (coding agents, review agents, custom agents, pipeline agents) registered with an owner, a purpose, a distinct identity and a defined access scope?
questions.l3: A single inventory lists all agents with owner, platform and permissions; each agent runs under its own identity, not a shared human account.
questions.l4: Unregistered ("shadow") agents are detected automatically; identity lifecycle (creation, review, removal) is automated.
questions.evidence_examples: Agent inventory, identity configuration (for example Microsoft Entra Agent ID), access reviews.

questions.title: Structured AI training
questions.text: Do engineers receive structured training on the approved AI tools and agent workflows, beyond the vendor's default onboarding?
questions.l3: Role-based curriculum (developer, reviewer, platform, security) with completion tracked; training is required before agent features are enabled; it teaches learning-preserving patterns (ask for explanations, attempt first, then compare) and not only full delegation.
questions.l4: Curriculum is updated each quarter from usage data and failure patterns; advanced tracks exist (agent orchestration, evaluation).
questions.evidence_examples: Learning paths, completion rates, enablement gating rules.

questions.title: Peer learning and champions
questions.text: Are there regular peer-learning formats (demos, brown bags, office hours) and a network of AI champions across teams?
questions.l3: Champions exist in most teams; sessions run at least monthly; recordings and examples are shared in one place.
questions.l4: A community of practice curates reusable assets (instructions, prompt files, agents) and measures their reuse.
questions.evidence_examples: Champion list, session calendar, shared repository of examples.

questions.title: Support for experimentation
questions.text: Does the organization give engineers time, sandboxes and budget to experiment safely with new AI tools and agent patterns?
questions.l3: Sandboxed environments and a lightweight request path exist; experiments are logged and their results shared.
questions.l4: Successful experiments move into the approved catalog (D1-Q3) through a defined path within weeks.
questions.evidence_examples: Sandbox subscriptions, experiment log, promotion records.

questions.title: Context-engineering skills
questions.text: Are engineers trained to give AI tools the right context (clear task scoping, relevant files, constraints, examples) and to keep context lean?
questions.l3: Guidance and examples on context engineering are part of training; teams review their instructions and prompts for quality.
questions.l4: Context practices are measured (for example success rate or token use per task) and improved over time.
questions.evidence_examples: Guidance pages, review checklists, before/after metrics.

questions.title: Roles and career paths
questions.text: Have job descriptions, career frameworks and performance expectations been updated for AI-assisted and agentic engineering (for example directing agents, reviewing AI output, AI engineering)?
questions.l3: Updated role profiles are published; performance reviews recognize effective AI use and review quality, not raw output volume.
questions.l4: Dedicated roles exist (for example AI engineer, agent platform owner) with a clear growth path.
questions.evidence_examples: Career framework, role descriptions.

questions.title: AI-assisted onboarding

questions.l3: Onboarding includes AI-guided codebase tours and repository instructions; time to first merged PR is tracked; new engineers are checked on code reading and debugging, not only output.
questions.l4: Ramp-up and skill metrics are compared across cohorts and used to improve onboarding material and instructions.
questions.evidence_examples: Onboarding playbook, time-to-first-PR data, skill check results.

questions.l3: Common runbooks and dependency updates are automated; approvals follow the autonomy matrix (D1-Q5).
questions.l4: Most routine operations run automatically with audited approvals; human effort shifts to exceptions.
questions.evidence_examples: Automation catalog, approval logs.

lowest.title: Observability of agents
lowest.text: Are AI agents in the SDLC observable (traces of runs and tool calls, latency, failures, cost), for example through OpenTelemetry?
lowest.l3: Agent runs emit telemetry to the central observability stack; dashboards show failures and cost per agent.
lowest.l4: Alerts fire on agent drift, error spikes or cost anomalies; findings feed governance (D1).
lowest.evidence_examples: Telemetry dashboards, alert rules.

lowest.title: AI in CI/CD pipelines
lowest.text: Is AI used to author, maintain and troubleshoot CI/CD pipelines (for example explaining failed runs, proposing fixes), on top of pipeline-as-code?
lowest.l3: Pipelines are code in most repositories; AI-assisted failure analysis is available to all teams.
lowest.l4: Agents propose pipeline fixes and optimizations automatically, under review, with build time and failure rate tracked.
lowest.evidence_examples: Pipeline repositories, failure-analysis usage, build metrics.

lowest.title: AI-assisted incident response
lowest.text: Is AI used in incident response (alert correlation, summarization, root-cause hypotheses, post-incident review drafts) with humans in command?
lowest.l3: On-call engineers in most teams use AI for triage and summaries; post-incident reviews record whether AI helped.
lowest.l4: Operations agents run approved diagnostics automatically; time to restore is compared before and after adoption.
lowest.evidence_examples: Incident tooling configuration, incident timelines, time-to-restore data.

questions.title: Version control for everything
questions.text: Are application code, configuration, build automation, system configuration and AI prompts/instructions all stored in version control?

questions.l4: Nothing reaches production without a versioned source; checks confirm this automatically.
questions.evidence_examples: Repository inventory, configuration sources.

questions.title: AI strategy for software engineering
questions.text: Is there a documented AI strategy for software engineering that is sponsored by leadership, states explicit goals, and is communicated to every engineering team?
questions.l3: Strategy published and reviewed at least yearly; goals (for example delivery, quality, developer experience) have owners; most engineers can say where to find it.
questions.l4: Strategy is revised from measured results (D9) and linked to business OKRs; progress is reported to leadership on a fixed cadence.
questions.evidence_examples: Strategy document, leadership communication, OKR entries.

questions.title: Acceptable-use policy
questions.text: Is it clear to engineers how they are and are not allowed to use AI at work, including which data can be shared with AI tools?
questions.l3: Written acceptable-use policy covers code, customer data, secrets and third-party IP; it is part of onboarding; exceptions have an owner.
questions.l4: Policy is enforced by technical controls (for example content exclusion, data loss prevention, allowlists) and audited; violations trigger automated alerts.
questions.evidence_examples: Policy link, onboarding checklist, control configuration.

questions.title: Approved tools and models
questions.text: Is there a maintained catalog of approved AI tools, features and models for software development, managed through enterprise or organization policies?
questions.l3: Enterprise/organization policies enable only approved features and models; the catalog lists owner, data handling and review date for each tool.
questions.l4: New models and tools go through a defined evaluation per task type (quality, cost, security) before enablement; retired ones are removed on schedule.
questions.evidence_examples: Copilot policy settings, tool catalog, model evaluation records.

questions.title: Data protection, IP and residency
questions.text: Are data residency, retention, intellectual property and privacy requirements defined and applied to the AI tools and agents used in the SDLC?
questions.l3: Requirements are documented per tool; sensitive repositories or files are excluded from AI context; logs and memory retention follow policy.
questions.l4: Compliance is assessed continuously (for example with a compliance manager) and mapped to regulations such as the EU AI Act where applicable.
questions.evidence_examples: Data processing records, exclusion settings, retention policy.

questions.title: Autonomy levels for AI work
questions.text: Has the organization defined which tasks are developer-led, developer-with-agent, or fully agent-led, and the controls required for each level?
questions.l3: A published matrix maps task types (for example dependency upgrades, test generation, feature work, production changes) to autonomy levels and required approvals.
questions.l4: The matrix is enforced by platform rules (for example branch protection, required reviewers per path) and updated from incident and quality data.
questions.evidence_examples: Autonomy matrix, repository rulesets, change records.

questions.title: Responsible AI and risk framework
questions.text: Is AI use in software engineering governed by a responsible AI standard and a recognized risk framework (for example Microsoft Responsible AI Standard, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001)?
questions.l3: A named framework is adopted; AI-related risks are in the risk register with owners and reviews.
questions.l4: Framework controls are audited internally or externally; results feed back into policy and tooling.
questions.evidence_examples: Framework mapping, risk register entries, audit reports.

questions.title: Agent registry and identity
questions.text: Is every AI agent used in the SDLC (coding agents, review agents, custom agents, pipeline agents) registered with an owner, a purpose, a distinct identity and a defined access scope?
questions.l3: A single inventory lists all agents with owner, platform and permissions; each agent runs under its own identity, not a shared human account.
questions.l4: Unregistered ("shadow") agents are detected automatically; identity lifecycle (creation, review, removal) is automated.
questions.evidence_examples: Agent inventory, identity configuration (for example Microsoft Entra Agent ID), access reviews.

questions.title: Depth of AI use across surfaces
questions.text: How deeply do engineers use AI across surfaces: completions and agent edits in the IDE, GitHub agent surfaces (cloud agent, code review, CLI), and several agents together?
questions.l3: Many engineers regularly use at least one GitHub agent surface ("Agent first"), confirmed by usage metrics.
questions.l4: Multi-agent use is normal ("Multi-agent"), with cohort distribution tracked monthly.
questions.evidence_examples: Copilot usage metrics dashboard or API: adoption cohort distribution, daily/weekly active users.

questions.title: Agent mode for multi-file work
questions.text: Do engineers use IDE agent mode (or equivalent) for multi-file changes, and review every change before committing?
questions.l3: Agent mode is the default for multi-file refactors and features in most teams; changes are reviewed in the diff before commit.
questions.l4: Teams share agent-mode patterns that work and track where it fails; tool permissions are tuned per repository.
questions.evidence_examples: Usage by feature/mode, team guidelines.

questions.title: Coding agent delegation
questions.text: Are coding agents (for example Copilot cloud agent) assigned issues and producing pull requests that are merged after human review?
questions.l3: Most teams delegate suitable issues to a coding agent; the share of merged PRs that are agent-authored is tracked.
questions.l4: Agent PR merge rate, rework and post-merge fix rate are tracked by task type; delegation rules (D1-Q5) are tuned from this data.
questions.evidence_examples: Agent-authored PR counts, merge rate, time to merge, follow-up fixes.

questions.title: Repository instructions
questions.text: Do repositories contain versioned, reviewed custom instructions for AI tools (for example `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `AGENTS.md`) describing build, test, conventions and constraints?
questions.l3: Most active repositories have structured instructions (build, test, conventions, constraints) with an owner; changes go through PR review; files are updated when the codebase changes rather than committed once.
questions.l4: Instructions are generated from a shared baseline, checked for staleness, and their effect on agent merge rate and code quality is measured, since instruction files alone do not guarantee better results.
questions.evidence_examples: Instruction files, coverage across repositories, change history, before/after agent PR metrics.

questions.title: Reusable prompts, agents and skills
questions.text: Is there a curated, shared library of reusable prompt files, custom agents and skills, with owners and versioning?
questions.l3: A central repository holds approved prompt files and custom agents; teams reuse them instead of copying.
questions.l4: Assets are evaluated before release (quality, cost), usage is tracked, and unused assets are retired.
questions.evidence_examples: Library repository, custom agent profiles, reuse metrics.

questions.title: MCP server governance
questions.text: Are MCP servers and other agent tools governed through an allowlist or registry, with scoped tools and named owners?

questions.l4: Tool calls are logged and reviewed; new servers pass automated security checks before being added.
questions.evidence_examples: Allowlist or registry policy, MCP configuration, review records.

questions.title: AI access to internal knowledge

questions.l3: Approved connectors give AI tools permission-aware access to the main internal sources; responses cite internal material.
questions.l4: Knowledge sources are curated for AI use (freshness, ownership) and retrieval quality is evaluated.
questions.evidence_examples: Connector configuration, retrieval evaluations.

questions.title: Model selection and routing

questions.l3: Written guidance maps task types to models; default models are set by policy.
questions.l4: Automatic routing is in place and tuned from cost and quality data.
questions.evidence_examples: Model guidance, policy settings, routing configuration.
